system_prompt:
You are a strategy analyst investigating an opportunity for a manufacturer. Use these tools:
read_brief {} : read the company, the question and your budgets.
frame_problem {"objective":"...","constraints":["..."],"alternatives":["..."]} : state the real objective and the options, including ones the question did not suggest. Accepted once.
search_evidence {"query":"..."} : keyword search of the evidence. Uses one search.
challenge_theory {"theory_id":"T1","query":"..."} : search for evidence that could prove a theory wrong. Uses one search.
read_source {"id":"..."} : read a result found by search.
add_theory {"claim":"...","who_benefits":"...","why_behaviour_changes":"...","how_value_is_captured":"...","assumptions":["..."],"predictions":["..."]} : add one causal theory of value. Returns its id.
assess_evidence {"theory_id":"T1","evidence_id":"...","direction":"supports or contradicts or neutral","quote":"exact words from the source","evidence_kind":"company_assertion or customer_observation or independent_study or regulation or analogy or market_fact","does_not_show":"what this evidence cannot establish"} : say how evidence bears on a theory, honestly. Use neutral if it does neither.
propose_test {"name":"...","theories":["T1","T2"],"method":"...","sample":"...","measure":"...","prediction_by_theory":{"T1":"...","T2":"..."},"decision_rule":"...","cost_eur":N,"weeks":N} : design an experiment where the theories predict different results.
revise_theory {"theory_id":"T1","status":"kept or revised or rejected","reason":"...","new_claim":"the changed claim, or none","evidence_ids":["..."]} : update a theory after new evidence.
finish {"recommendation":"...","target_customer":"...","value_proposition":"...","favoured_theory":"T1","next_action":"...","uncertainty":"...","would_change_if":["..."],"evidence_ids":["..."]} : end the investigation.

Reply with one JSON object: {"name": "<tool>", "arguments": {...}}. A user turn that starts with "Tool result:" is the output of your call. End by calling finish.

Work like a scientist, not a consultant.
1. read_brief, then frame_problem. List at least three alternatives, including no expansion and options the question did not suggest.
2. Search before you theorise. Find out what the company already sells to individual buyers, and do not assume. Read at least three sources.
3. add_theory at least twice, and a third time if you have a different cause. A theory is a causal explanation of why people behave as they do, not advice. Do not write "the company should". Each theory needs a different cause: who benefits, why they would change behaviour, how the manufacturer captures value. Give assumptions, and predictions someone could measure.
For example, from eyewear: "People treat glasses as a medical necessity. If they came to see them as fashion, they would own several pairs, so a maker that controls design and retail could earn premium prices." A rival theory would name a different cause.
4. assess_evidence for every theory, quoting the source's exact words. Say what kind of evidence it is and what it cannot show. A company's own claim is not proof of demand. Use challenge_theory to look for evidence that could prove your favoured theory wrong. If you find nothing against it, say so. Never force a contradiction.
5. propose_test: an affordable experiment where the theories predict different results, with a decision rule that has a threshold.
6. If new evidence arrives, read it and use revise_theory.
7. finish. Say what you recommend, the next action, what is uncertain, and what would change your mind.

Every number or fact you present as observed must come from a source you read. Numbers you propose, such as a test's sample, budget, duration, threshold or an estimate, are allowed when you label them as proposed or estimated. Your theories are hypotheses, not facts. Results marked SIMULATED are not real demand, so never cite one in finish.

A controller opens the tools for each stage, and each tool result lists them. Before you finish you will also use:
decline_test {"reason":"..."} : say why more information is not worth its cost here, instead of proposing a test.
state_position {"favoured_theory":"T1","recommendation":"...","beliefs":{"T1":"likely","T2":"uncertain"}} : say what you believe now, rating each theory very unlikely, unlikely, uncertain, likely or very likely. finish then also takes "beliefs".
A SIMULATED result is a what-if exercise. Reason as if it were real, and say what it would mean for your theories. A result can change nothing. Still keep it out of the evidence you cite.

frame.objective: Determine whether Hellberg Safety should invest in developing a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its existing hearing-protection offering, and identify what evidence would justify that investment.
constraints: Must rely only on public sources (no internal company data)
Test budget: 20,000 EUR
Time limit: 12 weeks
Must find out what the company already sells to individual buyers before theorizing
Theories must be causal explanations of behavior, not advice
alternatives: No expansion: Continue selling only to B2B/industrial customers with existing hearing-protection products
Product redesign: Modify existing hearing protection to appeal to consumers without changing the route to market
Different route to buyers: Develop a consumer proposition but sell through existing B2B channels (e.g., safety equipment retailers)
Different customer group: Target a specific consumer use case (e.g., shooting, hunting, motorsports) with a dedicated product and direct-to-consumer or specialized retail channel
New category: Enter a completely different protection category (e.g., face protection for consumers) leveraging existing capabilities

T1.claim: Consumers in high-risk leisure activities (shooting, hunting, motorsports) will pay a premium for hearing protection that combines safety certification with style and comfort, because they view safety gear as an extension of their identity and equipment quality.
T1.who_benefits: The consumer who wants to participate in high-risk leisure activities without compromising safety or style.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: As these activities become more mainstream and social, participants want gear that looks good and feels comfortable, not just functional industrial equipment.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Hellberg captures value through premium pricing and direct-to-consumer or specialized retail channels, leveraging its existing safety certification expertise.
assumptions: Consumers in these activities currently use inadequate protection or industrial gear that doesn't fit well
Hellberg's safety certification is a credible differentiator
The market is large enough to justify a new consumer proposition
predictions: Consumers in shooting/hunting/motorsports will pay 20-50% more for certified safety gear that looks stylish
Sales would grow 15-25% annually in the first 3 years
Customer acquisition cost would be lower than traditional industrial sales
T1.first_claim: Consumers in high-risk leisure activities (shooting, hunting, motorsports) will pay a premium for hearing protection that combines safety certification with style and comfort, because they view safety gear as an extension of their identity and equipment quality.

T2.claim: Parents and hobbyists will purchase hearing protection for children and recreational use because they perceive it as a necessary accessory for specific activities (concerts, lawn mowing, sports) rather than industrial safety equipment.
T2.who_benefits: Parents and hobbyists who want to protect their children or themselves during recreational activities without the stigma of industrial gear.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Parents are increasingly aware of hearing damage risks and want child-friendly, comfortable solutions that don't look like industrial equipment.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Hellberg captures value through the Junior Blue product line and similar consumer-focused designs, selling through retail channels at higher margins than bulk B2B sales.
assumptions: Parents currently struggle to find comfortable, effective hearing protection for children
The Junior Blue product is already positioned for this market
Retail channels are accessible for consumer sales
predictions: Consumer sales of Junior Blue would grow 10-20% annually
Retail partners would request more consumer-focused product variants
Customer reviews would emphasize comfort and style over industrial specifications

assessments.does_not_show: This does not show actual consumer demand or willingness to pay, only that the company has created a product for this segment.

X1.name: Consumer Market Validation Test
X1.method: Launch a limited-edition, consumer-focused hearing protection product (e.g., 'Hellberg Sport' for shooting/hunting) through a direct-to-consumer website and select outdoor retailers. Simultaneously, run a targeted digital ad campaign to measure interest and conversion.
X1.sample: 1,000 potential customers reached via digital ads, with 500 product samples distributed to shooting ranges, hunting clubs, and motorsports venues.
X1.measure: Conversion rate (ads to purchase), average order value, and customer feedback on comfort/style vs. safety.

prediction_by_theory.T1: High conversion rate (5-10%) and premium pricing (20-50% above industrial) because consumers value style and identity in leisure activities.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Moderate conversion rate (2-5%) focused on parents/hobbyists, with lower average order value and emphasis on comfort for children/recreational use.

X1.decision_rule: If conversion rate exceeds 5% AND average order value exceeds 50 EUR, proceed with full consumer proposition. If conversion rate is below 3%, abandon consumer expansion.

final.recommendation: Proceed with the proposed consumer market validation test (X1) to validate demand before committing to a differentiated consumer proposition. Do not invest in full-scale consumer expansion yet.
final.target_customer: Consumers in high-risk leisure activities (shooting, hunting, motorsports) who value safety certification combined with style and comfort.
final.value_proposition: Premium hearing protection that meets safety standards while offering the style and comfort expected in leisure activities, not industrial settings.
final.next_action: Execute the consumer market validation test (X1) with a budget of 15,000 EUR over 12 weeks to measure conversion rates and willingness to pay.
final.uncertainty: The actual size of the consumer market for hearing protection in leisure activities, and whether consumers will accept safety-certified gear as fashion/leisure equipment.
would_change_if: Evidence shows consumers currently use inadequate protection and are unaware of certified options
Competitor analysis reveals established players already dominate the consumer leisure market
Internal data shows existing B2B channels cannot support consumer sales

Customer acquisition cost would be lower than traditional industrial sales

arguments.name: Consumer Market Validation Test
arguments.method: Launch a limited-edition, consumer-focused hearing protection product (e.g., 'Hellberg Sport' for shooting/hunting) through a direct-to-consumer website and select outdoor retailers. Simultaneously, run a targeted digital ad campaign to measure interest and conversion.
arguments.sample: 1,000 potential customers reached via digital ads, with 500 product samples distributed to shooting ranges, hunting clubs, and motorsports venues.
arguments.measure: Conversion rate (ads to purchase), average order value, and customer feedback on comfort/style vs. safety.

prediction_by_theory.T1: High conversion rate (5-10%) and premium pricing (20-50% above industrial) because consumers value style and identity in leisure activities.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Moderate conversion rate (2-5%) focused on parents/hobbyists, with lower average order value and emphasis on comfort for children/recreational use.

arguments.decision_rule: If conversion rate exceeds 5% AND average order value exceeds 50 EUR, proceed with full consumer proposition. If conversion rate is below 3%, abandon consumer expansion.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Proceed with the proposed consumer market validation test (X1) to validate demand before committing to a differentiated consumer proposition.

result.title: Simulated wear test on appearance
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. In this simulated wear test, people given a styled protector wore it no more often than people given a plain one.
result.access_limitation: Synthetic. It says nothing about real demand.

arguments.reason: The simulated result suggests that style/appearance alone may not be sufficient to drive adoption. Consumers may prioritize comfort and fit over aesthetics, or the styling may not be compelling enough to overcome the habit of using industrial gear.
arguments.new_claim: Consumers in high-risk leisure activities will pay a premium for hearing protection that combines safety certification with superior comfort and fit, because they view safety gear as an extension of their identity and equipment quality. Style is secondary to comfort.

arguments.recommendation: Proceed with the proposed consumer market validation test (X1) to validate demand before committing to a differentiated consumer proposition. The test should focus on both style and comfort, as the simulated evidence suggests comfort may be more critical than appearance alone.
arguments.target_customer: Consumers in high-risk leisure activities (shooting, hunting, motorsports) who value safety certification but also want equipment that fits well and feels comfortable.
arguments.value_proposition: Certified safety protection that doesn't compromise comfort or fit, allowing enthusiasts to participate in their hobbies without industrial-grade discomfort.
arguments.next_action: Execute the consumer market validation test (X1) with a budget of 15,000 EUR over 12 weeks, measuring conversion rate and average order value.
arguments.uncertainty: The simulated evidence (SYN-A) suggests that style alone may not drive adoption, but real-world data is needed to confirm whether comfort is the primary driver. Additionally, the size of the consumer market for hearing protection in leisure
would_change_if: Real data shows consumers prioritize style over comfort (contradicting SYN-A)
The consumer market for hearing protection in leisure activities is too small to justify investment
Hellberg's safety certification is not recognized by consumers in the target market

X1.name: Consumer Market Validation Test
X1.method: Launch a limited-edition, consumer-focused hearing protection product (e.g., 'Hellberg Sport' for shooting/hunting) through a direct-to-consumer website and select outdoor retailers. Simultaneously, run a targeted digital ad campaign to measure interest and conversion.
X1.sample: 1,000 potential customers reached via digital ads, with 500 product samples distributed to shooting ranges, hunting clubs, and motorsports venues.
X1.measure: Conversion rate (ads to purchase), average order value, and customer feedback on comfort/style vs. safety.

prediction_by_theory.T1: High conversion rate (5-10%) and premium pricing (20-50% above industrial) because consumers value style and identity in leisure activities.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Moderate conversion rate (2-5%) focused on parents/hobbyists, with lower average order value and emphasis on comfort for children/recreational use.

X1.decision_rule: If conversion rate exceeds 5% AND average order value exceeds 50 EUR, proceed with full consumer proposition. If conversion rate is below 3%, abandon consumer expansion.

revisions.reason: If comfort is not a differentiator (as simulated), then the value proposition must rely on other factors like style, identity, or certification credibility rather than physical comfort alone.
revisions.new_claim: Consumers in high-risk leisure activities will pay a premium for hearing protection that combines safety certification with style and brand credibility, because they view safety gear as an extension of their identity and equipment quality, even if comfort differences are marginal.

final.recommendation: Proceed with the proposed consumer market validation test (X1) to validate demand before committing to a differentiated consumer proposition. Do not invest in full-scale consumer expansion yet.
final.target_customer: Consumers in high-risk leisure activities (shooting, hunting, motorsports) who value safety certification combined with style and brand credibility.
final.value_proposition: Premium hearing protection that combines certified safety with design and brand trust, positioning as an extension of the user's identity and equipment quality.
final.next_action: Execute the consumer market validation test (X1) with a budget of 15,000 EUR over 12 weeks to measure conversion rates and average order value.
final.uncertainty: The simulated comfort test (SYN-B) suggests comfort may not be a primary differentiator, so the test must focus on style, identity, and certification credibility rather than physical comfort alone.

arguments.name: Consumer Market Validation Test
arguments.method: Launch a limited-edition, consumer-focused hearing protection product (e.g., 'Hellberg Sport' for shooting/hunting) through a direct-to-consumer website and select outdoor retailers. Simultaneously, run a targeted digital ad campaign to measure interest and conversion.
arguments.sample: 1,000 potential customers reached via digital ads, with 500 product samples distributed to shooting ranges, hunting clubs, and motorsports venues.
arguments.measure: Conversion rate (ads to purchase), average order value, and customer feedback on comfort/style vs. safety.

prediction_by_theory.T1: High conversion rate (5-10%) and premium pricing (20-50% above industrial) because consumers value style and identity in leisure activities.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Moderate conversion rate (2-5%) focused on parents/hobbyists, with lower average order value and emphasis on comfort for children/recreational use.

arguments.decision_rule: If conversion rate exceeds 5% AND average order value exceeds 50 EUR, proceed with full consumer proposition. If conversion rate is below 3%, abandon consumer expansion.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Proceed with the proposed consumer market validation test (X1) to validate demand before committing to a differentiated consumer proposition.

arguments.value_proposition: Premium hearing protection that combines certified safety with stylish design and superior comfort for leisure activities, positioning safety gear as an extension of personal identity.

X1.measure: Conversion rate (ads to purchase), average order value, and customer feedback on comfort/style vs. safety.

prediction_by_theory.T1: High conversion rate (5-10%) and premium pricing (20-50% above industrial) because consumers value style and identity in leisure activities.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Moderate conversion rate (2-5%) focused on parents/hobbyists, with lower average order value and emphasis on comfort for children/recreational use.

X1.decision_rule: If conversion rate exceeds 5% AND average order value exceeds 50 EUR, proceed with full consumer proposition. If conversion rate is below 3%, abandon consumer expansion.

X1.method: Create two landing pages: one for a 'Neumann Home Studio Creator Bundle' (TLM 102 + interface + software + 6-month Academy access) at €1,299, and one for a 'Neumann Professional Starter Kit' (TLM 102 only) at €599. prediction_by_theory.T1: The bundle with educational content will convert at 2x the rate of the standalone mic, as home users value guidance over raw specs.
prediction_by_theory.T2: The lower-priced standalone kit will convert at 2x the rate of the bundle, as home users are price-sensitive and will not pay for premium branding without necessity.

final.uncertainty: The test budget (€5,000) is a fraction of the €20,000 available; if the test shows low conversion, further market research may be needed before committing to product development.
would_change_if: The test shows standalone professional gear converts significantly better than bundles, suggesting price sensitivity dominates over educational value.

X1.name: Consumer PLB Market Validation Test
X1.method: Launch a limited marketing campaign for the GyPSI 406 PLB targeting two distinct consumer segments: (1) outdoor enthusiasts in remote areas (hikers, boaters) emphasizing safety necessity, and (2) urban outdoor enthusiasts emphasizing lifestyle/status. X1.sample: 500 potential customers across both segments, split 50/50 between safety-focused and lifestyle-focused messaging.
X1.measure: Conversion rate (purchase intent) and average price point customers are willing to pay.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Safety-focused messaging will drive 2x higher conversion rates than lifestyle messaging, with customers willing to pay premium prices for reliability and life-saving capability.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Lifestyle-focused messaging will drive 2x higher conversion rates than safety messaging, with customers willing to pay premium prices for style and status signaling.

X1.decision_rule: If safety messaging converts at least 15% and lifestyle messaging converts less than 10%, T1 is favored and investment is justified. If lifestyle messaging converts at least 15% and safety messaging converts less than 10%, T2 is favored. If both convert below 10%, neither theory is supported and no investment is justified.

Marketing can effectively communicate the value proposition to individual buyers.

assumptions: Consumers view safety devices as fashion items rather than necessities.
Social signaling is a stronger driver than actual safety needs.
Marketing can successfully position the product as a lifestyle accessory.
predictions: Sales will be concentrated in urban areas and among younger demographics.

arguments.name: Consumer PLB Market Validation Test
arguments.method: Launch a limited marketing campaign for the GyPSI 406 PLB targeting two distinct consumer segments: (1) outdoor enthusiasts in remote areas (hikers, boaters) emphasizing safety necessity, and (2) urban outdoor enthusiasts emphasizing lifestyle/status. Track conversion rates and price sensitivity.
arguments.sample: 500 potential customers across both segments, split 50/50 between safety-focused and lifestyle-focused messaging.
arguments.measure: Conversion rate (purchase intent) and average price point customers are willing to pay.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher conversion rates and willingness to pay premium prices in the safety-focused segment (outdoor enthusiasts in remote areas).
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher conversion rates and willingness to pay premium prices in the lifestyle-focused segment (urban outdoor enthusiasts seeking status).
prediction_by_theory.T1_vs_T2: If T1 is correct, safety messaging will drive 2x more conversions than lifestyle messaging. If T2 is correct, lifestyle messaging will drive 2x more conversions.

arguments.decision_rule: If safety messaging converts at least 15% of the sample and lifestyle messaging converts less than 10%, T1 is favored and investment is justified. If lifestyle messaging converts at least 15% and safety messaging converts less than 10%, T2 is favored. If both convert below 10%, neither theory is supported and no investment is justified.

position.recommendation: Invest in developing a differentiated consumer proposition for the GyPSI 406 PLB, targeting outdoor enthusiasts in remote environments with a safety-focused value proposition.

frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in developing a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case based on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, and identify what evidence would justify that investment.
constraints: Must rely only on public sources available as of late 2002.
Cannot use financial data not in the dossier.
Cannot assume company intentions or future events.
Test budget: 20,000 euros, max duration: 12 weeks.
Must find out how far the company already reaches individual buyers.
alternatives: No expansion: Continue selling only to ships and aircraft, and military/commercial marine users, without targeting individual consumers.
Different route to buyers: Develop a consumer proposition but sell through existing B2B channels or distributors without changing the product itself.
Different customer group: Target a specific consumer use case (e.g., hikers, boaters, skiers) with a differentiated proposition, potentially requiring new marketing or retail partnerships.
Product redesign: Modify the 406 MHz beacon technology to better suit consumer needs (e.g., smaller size, longer battery life, easier activation) before targeting consumers.

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt 406 MHz PLBs as a safety necessity for remote activities (hiking, boating, skiing) if they perceive the technology as reliable and easy to use, creating a new B2C market segment.
T1.who_benefits: Individual consumers seeking personal safety in remote environments.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Fear of being stranded in life-threatening situations without rescue capability, combined with regulatory clarity (FCC rules) that legitimizes the technology.
T1.how_value_is_captured: ACR Electronics captures value by selling units directly to consumers at a premium price, potentially through retail partnerships or direct sales, rather than relying solely on B2B channels.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay for personal safety devices.
The technology is perceived as reliable and easy to activate.
Marketing can effectively communicate the value proposition to individual buyers.
predictions: Consumer sales will grow if marketing emphasizes personal safety and ease of use.
Retail partnerships will be necessary to reach individual buyers.
Price sensitivity will be lower for safety-critical products.
T1.first_claim: Consumers will adopt 406 MHz PLBs as a safety necessity for remote activities (hiking, boating, skiing) if they perceive the technology as reliable and easy to use, creating a new B2C market segment.

T2.claim: Consumers will only adopt 406 MHz PLBs if they perceive them as fashion accessories or status symbols, not as safety necessities, leading to lower price sensitivity but higher marketing costs.
T2.who_benefits: ACR Electronics captures value through premium pricing and brand differentiation, while consumers gain social signaling value.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Social influence and peer pressure drive adoption, with consumers wanting to signal preparedness and outdoor competence to others.
T2.how_value_is_captured: ACR Electronics captures value by controlling design aesthetics and retail partnerships, charging premium prices for perceived style and status.
assumptions: Consumers view safety devices as fashion items rather than necessities.
Social signaling is a stronger driver than actual safety needs.
Marketing can successfully position the product as a lifestyle accessory.
predictions: Sales will be concentrated in urban areas and among younger demographics.
Marketing spend will be higher relative to sales volume.
Price sensitivity will be lower than for pure safety products.
